subject: Prospective PhD student (Fall 2027): consent and what people think they've agreed to
body:
Dear Prof. Li,

I'm a master's student in data science at Lakeshore University, and I'm applying to Khoury's PhD program this cycle. I'm writing because the questions I want to study match your lab's work closely.

As a research assistant, I built bus ridership forecasts using location data from a third-party vendor. People had shared that data by tapping "allow" once in some app. It was anonymized and the use was allowed, but I doubted anyone tapping "allow" pictured their movements ending up in a transit agency's planning model. That gap between what people technically consented to and what they think they agreed to is what I want to study.

Your AuthorizationBench preprint caught my attention because it asks a similar question about agents: what someone authorized versus what is actually done on their behalf. CIDER's focus on contextual disclosure boundaries, and the lifecycle position paper's point that many privacy harms start at data collection, are also close to what I care about. So far my only work with people has been a small think-aloud study of an AutoML tool. In it, two participants assumed the tool already knew which of their data columns were sensitive. I'd like to do much more research of that kind.

Are you planning to take new PhD students for Fall 2027? I'd be glad to share my CV or talk briefly if that would be useful.

Best,
Morgan Reyes
M.S. Data Science, Lakeshore University
morgan.reyes@example.edu
